the movie was off to a good start, with the music, animation, and plot, even the setting taking place in 1929, pre-WW2, and within the timeframe of Italy joining Germany, all aligning well and coming out beautifully. i’ve questioned Ghibli writing a misogynistic lead and limiting men to brainless, women-obsessed creatures, as Ghibli is widely known for tender love, genuine connections, and respect amongst all genders, but it came to serve the greater good of proving the lead wrong and showing women gaining respect over and over again. a nice way to deliver an idea, until it wasn’t. Gina and Fio are truly the stars of the movie. even with how few scenes Gina got, she still showed up during the climaxes of the plot, often solving things herself. and then there’s Fio, the 17-year-old girl with ambitions to design airplanes and see the beauty of the world. i loved Fio so much. she’s ambitious, well-spoken, brave, and talented. i always love seeing a hardworking, decision-making woman in media, let alone when she’s young and charming too. the plot follows Marco, a pilot who has lost hope in humanity due to all the torture and pain he’s seen during the war, which left him with nothing but survivor’s guilt. as he’s seen “all the good ones die,” he turned into a pig, which people theorize is a way of showing him detaching from the pain of being human, experiencing loss, love, and joy. he gave up on who he once was and became an aimless pig, no longer who he was before and unsure of who to become. but being surrounded by Fio’s charm and heartwarming personality restored his faith in humanity, allowing him to leave Porco behind and become Marco again. hence the sentence, “Porco never showed his face again.” the airplane by Gina’s island also suggests she won her bet, and that the night visitor reciprocated her love, which he wouldn’t have done before due to his low self-esteem and guilt. he thought she deserved any of the pilots who died, but not him. he doesn’t even know why he survived that day. moving on from that fear of unworthiness, he flies higher than ever and loves Gina how she wants to be loved. it’s a beautiful view of the movie that really makes sense. but here comes the elephant in the room... the kiss. it’s important to note that Fio is 17 years old, and Marco is in his 30s, if not early 40s. they connect as family, whether that’s shown through familial banter and fights or even encouragement and support. Fio notes throughout the movie that she’s similar to Marco when he was her age, showcasing the experience gap between them. she’s just starting, and yet she kisses him in a way relatives shouldn’t kiss. whether that’s a hint towards Gina-Fio-Marco engaging in polyamory, or just to show the genuine, impulsive joy and love Fio feels, and how her love for Marco came from him allowing her to experiment, i genuinely don’t care. that was completely unnecessary. if anything, most people were confused as to why it would happen. if Gina were the one who kissed him, it would’ve helped the plot immensely. it would’ve made sense. but the writer(s) found a semi-incestuous way of making it work, and it completely ruined the movie. which is why it gets one star. pedophilia isn’t a good plot.

non riesco a mettere più di due stelle perché il modo in cui è rappresentato il legame tra Marco/Porco e Fio, per me, “overshadows” l’intera trama. ho guardato il film al cineforum del left camp, carico di mille aspettative accumulatesi negli anni (perché ne ho sempre sentito solo parlare bene), per poi ritrovarmi completamente spiazzato da quella dinamica di cui nessuno mi aveva mai proferito parola. da quando Marco/Porco mette piede nella Piccolo SRL, per me è stato un crescendo di disagio e disgusto, che per tutto il film mi ha fatto pensare “ma ora questa dinamica si smonterà, vero?”, per poi non smontarsi mai e anzi, peggiorare con il finale! ma dico io: che bisogno c’era di rendere la ragazzina 17enne l’oggetto della bramosia di decine di uomini adulti per tutto il film, senza rappresentarlo in modo critico? erano necessari i commenti sui suoi fianchi e sul suo sedere (!!) , o il modo in cui viene costantemente trattata come una ragazzina innamorata di un 36enne (Marco/Porco), che vuole a tutti i costi le sue attenzioni (anche chiedendogli di poterlo baciare, per poi pure farlo alla fine del film)? e ci tengo a mettere bene in chiaro una cosa: sono perfettamente consapevole del fatto che il film sia ambientato nel 1929 e pubblicato nel 1992. ciò non toglie che la dinamica tra i due personaggi potesse essere scritta in mille modi diversi da questo. il fatto che Fio abbia 17 anni e il legame con Marco non sia di tipo padre-figlia, bensì dipinto come un “rapporto speciale” più ambiguo, è una scelta DELIBERATA di rappresentazione della classica narrativa in cui “l’ amore di una ragazza candida e innocente, che vede il mondo con occhi diversi, è l’elemento salvifico del troubled man adulto di turno”. Porco letteralmente viene SALVATO dal bacio (sulla bocca) che gli dà Fio. ogni elemento, ogni scena che caratterizza questo lungo pattern che si dipana per tutta la pellicola, non è casuale, ma è lì per un motivo. simboleggia una rappresentazione ben precisa. e non è che il film è semplicemente “invecchiato male”, è che la cultura di base da cui parte non vede la problematicità di questa narrativa. e a questo mi collego a una critica più generale: è davvero impressionante vedere come queste narrative (che rimandano a ideali di p3dofilia, mi dispiace ma va detto: il pattern è lì, è visibile, gli elementi sono tanti e non è un semplice evento che si verifica una tantum nel film) siano sempre state così normalizzate, cioè viste come normali, da tanti, tantissimi uomini nell’industria cinematografica, così come in tutto il mondo. inutile dire che sono rimasto molto deluso da Miyazaki (anche se, alla fine, è sempre un uomo di una certa età…), e che penso non riuscirò a guardare i suoi film per qualche breve tempo. sono molto amareggiato, perché “la Principessa Mononoke” era entrato nella mia top 4 film di sempre, e ora francamente non mi sento molto a mio agio e a posto con me stesso nel metterlo lì. penso che lascerò quel posto ancora vacante per un po’. in conclusione, voglio dire che metto comunque due stelle anziché una perché, per onestà intellettuale, ci sono tante altre tematiche nel film che vengono trattate bene e che si meritano di non metterlo nella spazzatura dei film da una stella. ma qui si apre la riflessione su quello che più di tutto mi fa stare male: come è possibile che per anni ne avessi sentito soltanto tessere le lodi in giro, e davvero nessuno avesse pensato di muovere prima qualche critica riguardo a questo tema presente nel film? per me è un inferno vivere in un mondo in cui questo film è osannato (specialmente negli ambienti “compagni” e di sinistra, solo per quella cazzo di quote sull’antifascismo), soprattutto se acriticamente. mi fa sentire ancora più alienato nel mio disagio. spero che in futuro, se mi capiterà di guardare film in cui noto nuovamente questo tipo di dinamica/narrativa, questo succeda in compagnia di persone che hanno la mia stessa sensibilità su questo tema.

It was okay. Not entirely my cup of tea but the art is cosy as always. I did find it really irritating, though, with the constant inappropriate comments and behaviour towards Fio, an underaged girl. It genuinely kept taking me out of it. Even if it's supposed to reflect "a different time," that doesn't really change the outcome. I remember watching films as a kid where there were indirect and direct sexual comments about underage female characters, especially in children's films. It’s not only the middle aged men making these comments, they also show her playing along, even though most of the time she doesn’t enjoy it. The film doesn’t portray their actions as wrong either, as it is both the good and bad guys who do it, and it is also the fact that it happens CONSTANTLY throughout the film. It gets old very quickly. And let me tell you, that kind of thing does affect you A LOT as a kid. Especially as a young girl. It’s not empowering, it’s not with good intent. It makes you look at yourself in a completely different, and honestly devastating way. Those ideas stick with young girls and can follow them well into adulthood because we've been exposed to them and force-fed it since our developmental years. We are indoctrinated into this role of always having to be desirable to men regardless of age, and that this is the most important thing in our lives. I know it because I’ve lived it growing up, and it can take devastating forms. I don't think intention really matters in this case. Whether it was meant as a joke, a product of its time, or anything else, it's still icky, gross, and ultimately harmful.

The sequence where Marko/Porco sees his friends and enemies ascend to the clouds after their deaths was a really pretty sight. I love Ghibli films, but after rewatching Porco Rosso, I think it has major structural flaws. The film suffers from severe tonal whiplash—it tries to explore heavy themes like PTSD, survivor's guilt, and the anti-fascism, but constantly undercuts them with plain silliness. For instance, the sky graveyard scene is a haunting depiction of war trauma, but its emotional weight is completely undone by placing it alongside goofy slapstick and cartoonish pirate fights. Porco's transformation into a pig is clearly a metaphor for self-loathing, yet the movie treats his condition as a punchline far more often than a psychological burden. Furthermore, the treatment of Fio is deeply uncomfortable and unnecessary. She is introduced as a brilliant 17-year-old engineer, yet the plot constantly reduces her to an object of male desire. The climax literally turns her into a prize to be won in a fistfight between two older men, which completely strips away her agency. Finally, the film's politics feel superficial. Porco’s iconic line, 'I'd rather be a pig than a fascist,' sounds great, but his actual stance is just passive avoidance. He doesn't resist fascism; he just retreats to a private island to work as a mercenary. Using anti-fascism as an aesthetic backdrop without engaging in actual resistance makes the slogans feel empty. Also this film was catered towards middle age men — it started off as a short in - flight film for airlines. So just by this alone it makes the whole Fio thing worse. To this day, I still can’t quite say where I should place Porco Rosso amongst the other Ghibli films. On the one hand, it’s a visually stunning film with plenty of aviation action, beautiful scenes set on the island and out across the sea, and a great deal of heart. But on the other hand, the story is actually very simple and centres on a feud between two pilots and the road to their ultimate showdown. Just between the lines, Porco Rosso repeatedly offers bits of information that add depth to the world and its characters. However, these are very rarely explored in any real detail. Porco Rosso is definitely worth a watch for fans of the studio, but it’s more of a light-hearted slice-of-life film that’s great fun whilst you’re watching it, yet doesn’t leave much of a lasting impression the days after.

a cena do "cemitério de aviões" é arrebatadora. daquelas que deslumbram, mas, ao mesmo tempo, te devoram. para mim, é uma das melhores de todo o estúdio. as sequências de voo também são impressionantes. nelas, dá para ver a paixão de miyazaki pela aviação em cada detalhe de capricho. sinto que "porco rosso" é quase como sua carta de amor aos aviões. porco é um homem que deixou de ser humano em um mundo cada vez mais desumanizado. trata-se de uma amálgama metafórica entre a visão que ele tem de si mesmo por carregar a culpa de ser um sobrevivente no pós-guerra e o abismo que se cria entre ele e a sociedade. ele voluntariamente se transforma em uma figura socialmente indesejada, pois prefere abdicar de seu status e de sua própria forma humana a se curvar e servir a um regime autoritário. fica evidente como, para miyazaki, o ato de voar sempre foi a representação máxima da liberdade e da beleza humana. os céus, antes ocupados por "aviadores românticos", agora passam a ser uma mera ferramenta de propaganda militar. mas, ainda assim, não consegui deixar de me incomodar com a relação entre porco e fio. a audácia e o otimismo inabalável dela na humanidade são as forças responsáveis por fazer com que marco, posteriormente, comece a fazer as pazes consigo mesmo. enquanto marco, engolido pelo nacionalismo vazio, escolhe se isolar em seu pessimismo e acreditar que "todos os homens bons morreram", fio representa o amanhã, incorporando a juventude que carrega o espírito revolucionário de recusa à imutabilidade que aparenta estar posta. em um primeiro momento, tudo isso me pareceu meio nebuloso e senti que a mensagem perdia força com essa relação ambígua entre os dois. ao mesmo tempo que se constrói uma postura quase paternal quando ele repreende as atitudes dos homens ao redor que a objetificam constantemente, o filme reforça a atração que ele sente por ela em diversas vezes. essa dubiedade estética e narrativa me impediu, inicialmente, de comprar a dinâmica entre os personagens e de me cativar por eles por completo. mas mudei de perspectiva quando soube o que o próprio miyazaki falou sobre a obra. sabendo que ele declarou que todos os homens de meia-idade se transformam em porcos, e que projetou no protagonista suas próprias frustrações, passei a ver essa dubiedade com outros olhos. percebi que ela reflete uma escolha de sobrepor o embate ideológico limpo a uma autocrítica muito crua da masculinidade. marco é um herói político firme, mas moralmente rústico e impregnado pelo cinismo de seu tempo. esse contraponto é evidente até na vida real. nem mesmo os nossos heróis históricos estavam limpos dessa sujeira da época em que viviam. ao escancarar as contradições do personagem em vez de poupá-lo, a obra nos lembra que mesmo as figuras mais avançadas politicamente carregavam pontos cegos, e revela como é fundamental para as novas gerações encarar e superar essa herança ultrapassada por dentro dos próprios movimentos de mudança. antes eu ia dizer que não tinha gostado tanto, mas agora sinto que gosto do filme. preciso rever com outros olhos para me decidir por completo.

being that she's 17 and he's both a pig and whatever age he's supposed to be. i was much more interested in his relationship with madame gina, and then fio's story of overcoming gender prejudices (i laughed a lot at " god forgive us for having women fixing these planes ") and showing her resourcefulness in this male dominated world of pirates and planes that being said, there are some really great moments in here that spark some of that usual ghibli magic. first of all, i really loved the generally optimistic tone of the piece. considering it's dealing with some heavy themes, of ptsd, pirates and fascism (i'd rather be a pig than a fascist too), it juxtaposes this nicely with a lot of lightness. was smiling ear to ear at the girls' swim team when they were kidnapped, generally causing a nuisance and being overly curious. and i loved the family of women fixing the plane, and the crew of pirates who also had super wholesome vibes. despite the film feeling so small in scope, it does feel like there's lots of potential with these different groups of characters for humour and interesting stories. i even liked the american and his constantly falling in love with every woman he met. his rivalry with porco was pretty funny and sweet too and the animation looks pretty nice. i love the post ww1 italian aesthetic, so gorgeous. enjoyed the animated film within a film at the movie theatre too, really fun concept seeing ghibli doing a different style. perhaps my favourite scene in the entire thing though, in terms of both storyline and imagery, was the concept of the plane heaven, with all the planes converging to form one giant chemtrail essentially. a really beautiful concept - i always love in films and television when different subgroups and cultures have their own concept of a heaven that's extremely niche and specific. it's the kind of thing where if i'd watched this as a kid i'd probably have been preoccupied with the plane fights and the talking pig, and only noticed just how touching this moment is on later watches as an adult. perhaps if i wasn't in such a fidgety mood, it might have even elicited tears. guess we'll have to find out on a rewatch! enjoyed the score too, particularly the italian songs sung by madame gina. the quiet sadness of her storyline really moved me, though i wish she had been developed more. appreciated the ambiguity of her ending, as well as the question around if porco transformed back or not. i think it's indicated that he did, but i appreciate that we never see it on screen for sure. same thing with him coming back for madame gina - maybe i missed it but i think it was kept pretty ambiguous if he just went on the run forever or if he went back for her and declared his love. but either way, kinda makes me wish the porco/fio relationship had more father/daughter overtones. still works with the kiss restoring him, but leaves room for greater focus on his relationship with madame gina, even if the ending is left ambiguous still overall think this will probably rank reasonably low once i've seen all the ghibli/miyazaki movies, but that doesn't mean it doesn't have some really touching moments that i've come to expect from these movies. i just think perhaps i'm not super interested in the world war aspect of history, and i find the plane fights can only keep me entertained for so long. while i find a lot of the characters to be pretty sweet, and often interesting, it's maybe too male-focused for me to fully invest in. i think if i had seen this when i was younger i might have found it a bit boring, as i think the strength of the film lies in some of the quieter moments, and the deeper adult themes it has, like the rise of fascism, coming home changed from the horrors of war, and even the concept of plane heaven. but it still gets a strong rating (3.75 rounded up to 4 stars) as i thought it was an entertaining film! just suffers a bit in comparison to the heights i know this studio can usually reach!

I’d rather be a pig than a fascist This iconic line rings true today more than ever. As we are once again entering an era where world leaders are clamoring for power and dismantling democracy left and right. We are once again entering an era where young men and women are shipped off to war, and genocide is allowed to take place on full display. There are two main themes or thoughts, I guess, that stick with me from this film. And I’ve always enjoyed this commentary from the film. But re-watching it now for the first time in at least 15 years these hit so much harder: First off, the horrors of war and their impact on a person. There’s a famous quote that goes something along the lines of “no one ever survives a war, the person who returns is not the same one that left”. Porco Rosso himself is a LITERAL allegory for this, he is no longer a man but a pig. He is forever detached from reality, which impacts himself put also the people with whom he had previous relations. Secondly, this film about sea plane pilots on the Adriatic coast gives off many similar vibes to various westerns and films about pirates. The value of freedom is tremendous in a world which is shrinking, to the point where being broke (or literally being a pig) is a price worth paying. But this freedom is threatened by rapidly encroaching imperial movement. I really like the parallels between the airplanes in this film and the ships in media such as One Piece or Pirates of the Caribbean. What a ship is, is freedom. I be yearning for some sort of vessel where I can vanish over the horizon, capturing my freedom. This film is also very interesting due to Miyazaki's personal ambivalence and kind of embarassment to this film. He has many times called the film "foolish" and deemed it very self-indulgent and targeted at the wrong audience. A personal goal of Miyazaki's when making film is said to be to create worlds of escapism and childlike wonder. Where his works can, and often do, handle quite real and dark themes, but at the core there should be hope and childlike wonder. Porco Rosso however contrasts this, as there is no real "happy ending". Rather it leaves off quite melancholic and ambiguous, he doesn't become human and get the girl. As well as the meat of the story focusing on our grumpy middle-aged protagonist.

Porco Rosso é o filme mais melancólico e adulto do Miyazaki, e é justamente por isso que ele funciona tão bem. A premissa é absurda, um piloto da Primeira Guerra Mundial que foi transformado em porco, mas o filme trata isso com uma naturalidade que faz você esquecer a estranheza em minutos e simplesmente aceitar que aquele homem escolheu ser um porco porque o mundo dos humanos o decepcionou demais. A beleza do filme está nas coisas que ele não diz. A guerra, o amor não resolvido com Gina, a recusa de Marco em voltar à forma humana, tudo é tratado com uma leveza que esconde uma tristeza profunda, e é nesse contraste que o filme brilha. As cenas de voo são lindas, a animação é impecável e a atmosfera do Adriático te transporta de um jeito que poucos filmes conseguem. A ressalva é que o filme é mais contemplativo do que narrativo, e quem espera um arco dramático mais definido pode sentir falta de uma resolução mais clara, já que Miyazaki prefere deixar tudo em aberto, como a própria vida... No fim, Porco Rosso é um filme sobre desilusão e sobre a escolha de se isolar quando o mundo já não faz sentido. É leve na superfície e pesado por baixo, e é exatamente isso que o torna especial. E eu amo de fato, esta frase abaixo. "Eu prefiro ser um porco a ser um fascista."

(English Dub) I got to crack open my Steelbook today and I got so much joy out of this amazing, underrated film… This is often said to be Miyazaki’s anomaly, being originally adult-geared. It was apparently even made for Japanese businessmen returning home by flight to kick back and relax to. Miyazaki regretted making it because he felt it was too personal to him, his aspirations, and his own feelings rather than being universal to children and people in general. It’s a film that isn’t about a young person, and it isn’t even close to being a coming of age story. Porco is a middle aged cynical anthropomorphic pig with war guilt and self-esteem issues. There is mention of fascism, booze and cigarettes aplenty, and characters who womanize and disrespect women (critically, not transgressively). It’s quite real for a Ghibli film, and is a far cry away from the usual escapist nature of many other films by the studio. However, those dogfights, the hero plot/admirable protagonist, and some of the silly moments seem like they would have made me obsessed with this film as a kid, compelling me to constantly come back to it as I often did with movies I loved. The scenery and slow, steady pace of some of the shots just made me smile. The shots of the sea, the planes flying over it, and the Italian villages were truly meditation through art for me. The scene with the fallen pilots rising above the clouds might be the most beautiful thing I have seen in an animated film, period. And then of course Porco, the ultimate sigma (lol). Michael Keaton added an element to the character that worked so well. The character, with the help of Keaton’s iconic swagger behind the mic, is the reason this film works for audiences of all ages. Sarah loved the voice for “Boss” the gang leader, and thought he stood out from the rest. I must agree, but I think all the English dub voice actors involved did a fantastic job. The score was excellent too as it usually is in Miyazaki’s films, and very fitting to the environment and events. Overall, Porco Rosso checks every box whether the viewer is a child or an adult. It’s got love, it’s got funny American and Italian stereotypes, it’s got a lovable and ordinary hero who’s also fairly relatable, it’s got semi-historical war themes, and it’s got action with high stakes but also treated with a certain childish lightness to it. For Porco, it’s got self-reflection, hurdling obstacles, and learning to respect yourself all in one. We need more animated films like this. What upsets me is that we’ve abandoned carefully crafted slow-paced reflective art for children with cheap, addictive slop that disguises itself as educational. We can only hope that Miyazaki, and eventually new Ghibli producers, directors, and artists keep this legendary style alive to continue to inspire kids with these kinds of films for generations.
